title: Galaxy Clusters and Gravitational Lenses
objective: After this level you can describe galaxy clusters and how their gravity bends light.
summary: Galaxies gather in clusters of hundreds or thousands. Their gravity bends light, magnifying galaxies behind them.

cards.headline: Some of the universe’s best telescopes are made of gravity.
cards.body: No glass, no mirrors, no launch date. Just an enormous amount of mass, bending light on its way to us.

cards.headline: Cities of galaxies
cards.body: Galaxies aren't sprinkled evenly across space. Many gather into clusters of hundreds or thousands of galaxies, bound together by gravity. If the Local Group from Level 84 is a small town, a cluster is a city. And remember Level 85: there's roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter, so much of the gravity holding a cluster together comes from dark matter.

cards.headline: Bending light
cards.body: Einstein's relativity predicts that mass bends light. Pile up enough mass and you get a lens. A massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light of galaxies far behind it, like a magnifying glass held up to the deep universe. Webb's first deep-field image, released in 2022, used exactly this trick: a cluster in front magnified much more distant galaxies behind it. Free zoom, courtesy of gravity.

cards.fact: Most of a cluster's lens is invisible.
cards.context: With roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter, most of the mass bending that light gives off, absorbs and reflects no light at all. So the lens is mostly something we can't see. Astronomers are peering through an invisible magnifying glass.
